prospects.name: Critical Thinking
prospects.fit: An unusually close match for a technical conversation about browser security and web testing.
prospects.evidence: The official site lists episode 193 on browser logic errors and XS-Leaks, with Jorian Woltjer. Its episode notes publish the contact address.
prospects.angle: How browser research becomes a repeatable web-testing method
prospects.subject: Critical Thinking X Web Hacking Arsenal
prospects.message:
Hi Critical Thinking team,

Your episode with Jorian Woltjer on browser logic errors and XS-Leaks caught my attention, particularly given the overlap with Rafay Baloch’s work in browser and web application security.

I’m Ruth, helping Rafay with outreach around his book, Web Hacking Arsenal: A Practical Guide to Modern Web Pentesting.

Rafay is a cybersecurity researcher, author and founder of REDSECLABS. His research has included browser security vulnerabilities and CVEs, with previous work covered by outlets including the BBC and TechCrunch, and he has presented his research at conferences including Black Hat.

Rather than doing a conventional book interview, I thought there could be a strong technical conversation around how researchers move from unusual browser behaviour to exploitable security findings, where conventional web pentesting methodologies miss logic and browser-side issues, and how modern testers can develop better hypotheses rather than relying primarily on scanners and checklists.

The discussion could naturally draw on practical examples and techniques from Web Hacking Arsenal, which is focused on modern, hands-on web application penetration testing.

Would that be of interest for an upcoming episode? I’d be happy to send over a short outline with a few possible technical angles.

Best,
Ruth Maclang
Outreach for Rafay Baloch

prospects.subject: Application Security Weekly X Web Hacking Arsenal
prospects.message:
Suggested show: Application Security Weekly
Guest: Rafay Baloch
Proposed topic: From an isolated web finding to an actionable AppSec test

Reason:
Your recent discussion on moving from bug bounty bugs to more secure systems is a strong fit for a practical follow-on. Rafay is the author of Web Hacking Arsenal and is open to a technical discussion drawing on web application and browser-security work.

How to document a finding clearly, test the assumptions around it in an authorized environment, and turn that learning into a useful regression check for developers. The proposed discussion would use examples agreed with Rafay and focus on engineering lessons.

Submitter: Ruth Maclang, coordinating author outreach. Please route scheduling through me initially.

prospects.name: Software Engineering Radio
prospects.fit: A technical engineering podcast that explicitly accepts topic proposals with five points or an abstract.
prospects.evidence: Guidelines favor one practical, vendor-neutral topic, require supporting work and ask for an archive check. The editor email was read from the official page’s mail link. Its stated queue makes it a longer-term opportunity.
prospects.angle: Browser trust boundaries explained for working software engineers
prospects.subject: Software Engineering Radio X Web Hacking Arsenal
prospects.message:
Hi Robert,

I’m Ruth, coordinating outreach for Rafay Baloch, author of Web Hacking Arsenal. Following your topic-proposal format, I’d like to propose a discussion of browser trust boundaries for web engineers:

• How browser security assumptions influence application design.
• Where developers should distinguish client behavior from server-enforced controls.
• How to turn an observed browser behavior into a testable security question.
• What evidence makes a finding reproducible and useful to developers.
• How to carry that learning into regression testing.

Rafay is open to a practical, vendor-neutral discussion. Supporting work: Web Hacking Arsenal, published by CRC Press, and its public companion repository. We would agree concrete examples with him before recording.

Would this topic be worth developing for the show?

Best,
Ruth Maclang
Outreach for Rafay Baloch
